newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Indian minister sees better ties with Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Indian minister sees better ties with Bangladesh.

text.p: Indian Foreign Minister I.K. Gujral reaffirmed on Sunday that his country wanted to resolve a nagging water sharing dispute with Bangladesh.

"It's our intention that before the next lean season (December) comes in we should have arrived at some understanding to the satisfaction of Bangladesh to a larger extent," Gujral told Indian reporters accompanying him.
He was talking to the reporters at a 45-minute meeting with Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina when he handed her a letter from Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Bangladesh wants increased waters from the river Ganges, the flow of which is controlled by India through its Farakka Barrage, 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's northern border.
On Saturday Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad told reporters after talks with Gujral that Dhaka expected a solution regarding water sharing by the next lean period.
"I endorse what he (Azad) is saying," Gujral said, indicating that Dhaka and Delhi expect an agreement by December.

Under the last agreement which expired in 1988, Bangladesh received 34,500 cusecs (cubic feet per second) of Ganges water during the dry season. Attempts to renew the agreement have since failed, with Dhaka insisting on taking at least 80 percent of the lean-season flow.
Sharing of water from the Ganges, called Padma in Bangladesh, has long been a major irritant in relations between the two unequal south Asian neighbours.
Officials claim that more than 40 million people in northwestern Bangladesh have faced gradual desertification of their land since the Farakka was commissioned in 1974.
Gujral said on Sunday he expected his country's relations with Dhaka would improve under the new government of Bangladesh.
"We have given a major concession. We have agreed to abolish all non-tariff barriers and reduced the 50 percent tariff on a large number of Bangladeshi items," Gujral said.

Gujral said Bangladesh was going to support India's bid for a temporary seat in the U.N. Security Council later this year and understood India's veto of a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty in Geneva last month.
Gujral said Bangladesh had also given an assurance that it would not allow "any anti-Indian activity from its soil..."
The Indian minister's visit was the first high-level contact between Dhaka and New Delhi after Hasina took office following an election victory in June.
Gujral said he also discussed with the Bangladeshi prime minister the issue of Chakma refugees and regional and international matters.

Up to 50,000 Chakmas fled to northeast India over the past five or six years from Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, where troops have been fighting a fledgling tribal insurgency since 1973. Some 6,000 Chakmas were repatriated in 1994 and several thousands have returned on their own, officials said.
